title: Why the Sea Never Runs Out
question: How do chemical elements keep moving through the ocean and the life in it?
hook: Sea life uses nitrogen and phosphorus all the time, so why doesn't the ocean run dry of them?
idea: Elements are never created or destroyed, so they keep cycling between seawater, air, seafloor, land and living things, while energy passes through and leaves as heat.

beats.prompt: Farms along a major river spread nitrate fertilizer, and rain washes much of it off the fields. What happens where the river reaches the sea?

choices.label: A dead zone forms at the river's outlet
The nitrate is destroyed in the river
choices.feedback: Elements cannot be destroyed by these processes; runoff and rivers carry them along instead.

choices.label: The sea absorbs it with no visible effect
choices.feedback: At the mouth of the Mississippi, the fertilizer nitrates have produced a dead zone.

beats.explain: Runoff carries nitrogen from land to water, and fertilizer nitrates funnelled down the Mississippi have created a dead zone in the Gulf of Mexico.

beats.prompt: Sort each process by what it does to the ocean's saltiness.
beats.explain: Evaporation and sea ice formation push salinity up, while fresh water from rivers, rain, snow and melting ice brings it down.

beats.prompt: Match each element to a job it does in living things.
beats.explain: Each of these common elements is used by organisms in a different way.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: Sunlight brings energy into the ocean's food chains.
At each step up a food chain, some energy leaves as heat.
The carbon and nitrogen in sea creatures is also used up and must be made anew.
So energy flows one way while matter keeps cycling.
beats.explain: Elements can be neither created nor destroyed by these processes; the matter in organisms is conserved and recycled, unlike energy.
